original_value: AbstractAs the COVID‐19 pandemic has unfolded, Hate Speech on social media about China and Chinese people has encouraged social stigmatization. For the historical and humanistic purposes, this history‐in‐the‐making needs to be archived and analyzed. Using the query “china+and+coronavirus” to scrape from the Twitter API, we have obtained 3,457,402 key tweets about China relating to COVID‐19. In this archive, in which about 40% of the tweets are from the U.S., we identify 25,467 Hate Speech occurrences and analyze them according to lexicon‐based emotions and demographics using machine learning and network methods. The results indicate that there are substantial associations between the amount of Hate Speech and demonstrations of sentiments, and state demographics factors. Sentiments of surprise and fear associated with poverty and unemployment rates are prominent. This digital archive and the related analyses are not simply historical, therefore. They play vital roles in raising public awareness and mitigating future crises. Consequently, we regard our research as a pilot study in methods of analysis that might be used by other researchers in various fields.

result.paraphrase: AbstractAs the COVID-19 pandemic developed, hate speech on social media aimed at China and Chinese people has fostered social stigma. For historical and humanistic reasons, this history-in-the-making must be archived and analyzed. By querying “china+and+coronavirus” through the Twitter API, we collected 3,457,402 key tweets about China related to COVID-19. In this archive, with about 40% of tweets coming from the U.S., we identify 25,467 hate speech instances and examine them with machine learning and network methods, using lexicon-based emotions and demographics. The findings show substantial links between the volume of hate speech and expressions of sentiment, as well as state demographic factors. In particular, surprise and fear, tied to poverty and unemployment rates, are prominent. This digital archive and its analyses are not merely historical; they also help raise public awareness and mitigate future crises. Accordingly, we view our research as a pilot study in analytical methods that may be useful to other researchers across fields.
